body.text: Markets live updates: Qantas shares rise after Accenture deal, job cuts announced
Qantas will cut 850 jobs beginning mid-2027, with CEO Vanessa Hudson saying the airline has struck an outsourcing deal with Accenture.
Wall Street indices have leapt despite a spy scandal at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company.
Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.
Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
Qantas to cut 850 roles as it strikes outsourcing deal
Qantas says it will cut 850 roles in the coming years with the first changes expected mid-2027.
An email from Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson announced a multi-year partnership with tech firm Accenture and said the changes would affect parts of the company's corporate functions.
"While there are important reasons behind today’s news, I know that doesn't make the impact on our people any easier," she said.
"We expect around 850 roles to be affected over the coming years, with the first changes expected to be in place by mid-2027.
"Individual outcomes have not been determined and we will now work through consultation with affected employees and their union over the next few months."
New: Filters

Anthropic IPO aiming to raise up to $US69.3 billion: Reuters
Anthropic is aiming to raise as much as $US69.3 billion in what could rank among the largest initial public offerings on record, according to a copy of a filing seen by Reuters on Monday.
Reuters reported that shares will be priced in the range of $US70-80.
It also said Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, TSMC will invest $US26 billion through a private placement at IPO price.
When first unveiled last month, analysts described the looming float as a "watershed event" for tech and the AI revolution:
Qantas shares jump following announcment
Following the news of Qantas Group's partnership with Accenture, shares have jumped up 3.7%.
ASX reaches highest level since August

Australian shares have climbed to their highest level in more than two months on, with heavyweight miners leading gains, while lower oil prices eased inflation concerns and supported broader market sentiment.
The ASX 200 was up 0.8% at 9,099.90, as of about 10:30am (AEDT), its highest level since late August.
Global risk appetite was bolstered by US President Donald Trump downplaying the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran, which sent crude prices tumbling more than $7 to hit late-August lows.
Surging oil prices have fuelled inflationary pressures in economies around the world, including Australia, since the war began earlier this year.
Australian miners jumped 1.2%, aided by a rebound in copper prices.
Shares of BHP Group and Rio Tinto advanced 1.1% and 0.9%, respectively.
Gold miners also advanced, tracking stronger bullion prices.
What is petrol costing where you are?
OK, so the national average price of a litre of unleaded petrol is down 2.9 cents to 234.5 cents in the week to Sunday.
But what you really want to know is what it’s like where you live?
And thanks to the dedicated boffins at the Australian Institute of Petroleum, here’s that very data.
Qantas jobs to be replaced by jobs in India
Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson said the redundancies were part of a new multi-year partnership with Accenture pointing to the "scale and speed of change in technology".

"AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime," she said."It is changing what our customers expect from us and what you need from the tools you use every day, and leading businesses around the world, in aviation and beyond, are moving quickly. Standing still is not an option for us."
"AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime," she said.

"It is changing what our customers expect from us and what you need from the tools you use every day, and leading businesses around the world, in aviation and beyond, are moving quickly. Standing still is not an option for us."
She said Qantas would invest more than $1 billion a year in technology and the largest fleet renewal in the company's history.

"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," Ms Hudson said."It will allow us to unlock innovation faster and accelerate our use of AI, with lasting benefits."
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," Ms Hudson said.
"It will allow us to unlock innovation faster and accelerate our use of AI, with lasting benefits."
She said the two companies would work to "redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication".
The first phase of redundancies will affect Finance, Procurement, and People and Marketing, with some of these jobs being moved to Accenture's team, mostly in India.
Qantas has said it will look to redeploy as many people as possible.
Petrol falls 2.9 cents in a week
The national average price of a litre of unleaded petrol slid 2.9 cents to 234.5 cents in the week to Sunday.
Weekly data from the Australian Institute of Petroleum details the fall, which puts the average well above the 12-month average figure of 196.4 cents.
Top mover is Monadelphous
Mining services company Monadelphous* is the biggest gainer on the ASX 200 today, on the back of a first half revenue of $1.7 billion and a strong expected forecast result in the coming half.
No relation to Snuffleupagus
Life360 shares down 8.2%

Tech company Life360 has increased revenue 40% to $US174 million in the third quarter of its financial year and now has 107.7 monthly active users (MAU), which is the standard way tech companies report who is actually using their services.
And the market says NO.
Here's Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at etoro, on why that might be so:

"Life360 has delivered the growth investors were looking for, but the market isn’t quite ready to give it credit, with shares down around 6% in early ASX trade. Revenue grew 40% to USD$174 million, while operating costs fell to 72% of revenue from 80% just three months earlier. That’s an encouraging sign for a business that has been punished for spending ahead of its growth, but one quarter of improvement clearly hasn’t put those concerns to bed.

"The all-important subscription business is still firing on all cylinders. Life360 added a record 188,000 paying circles for a September quarter, and it’s lifting what each of those households pays, with the US price rises only just starting to flow through. Growing the paying base and the price tag together is exactly what you want to see from a subscription business, and it's not always easy to do. With more than 100 million people opening the app every month, there’s still a long way to go when it comes to converting free users into paying ones.

"Ad revenue more than tripled to USD$25 million, but that’s largely thanks to the Nativo acquisition rather than organic growth. Those advertising dollars also carry much thinner margins than subscriptions, which weighed on gross margin this quarter. Life360 is pinning its hopes on advertising becoming a second growth engine in 2027, but management trimmed the top end of its full-year ad forecast even as it lifted the floor on overall revenue guidance, so for now subscriptions are still doing the heavy lifting.

"Life360 has shown it can grow quickly while bringing costs down, but the investors will want to see that progress sustained. The next test is whether it can keep subscription growth strong and turn advertising into a meaningful second engine without putting fresh pressure on margins."
At the time of writing, shares in Life360, one of the few tech companies on the Australian stock market, are $20.48, down 8.3% today.
'Our final, most soul-destroying humiliation': Nick Cave on AI song generation
The Red Hand Files is a site where music legend Nick Cave answers questions from his fans.
It's no surprise that it is filled with entertaining and deep thoughts from the Dark Prince of music.

This week he answered two questions together. One was whether art could be separated from its maker (potentially in response to the sentencing of comic actor Russell Brand) and about whether he was a "doomer or boomer" on AI.
I've put some notes in parentheses () to elaborate, but otherwise, here's his response:
"Dear Nuno and Catherine,

"I have indeed spoken about separating the art from the artist a number of times in these Files, yet the question persists and remains an ethical tension for many people. How is it that some of the most beloved and beautiful works of art can be created by people of decidedly dubious character? We look at a (painting by) Caravaggio in a museum, a work of spiritual radiance but created by a murderer. We think we should perhaps turn away, but beauty holds us. We stand awed and baffled that even in such a character, a point of goodness exists from which great art can spring.

"Nuno, we cannot separate the art from the artists, for they are as inseparable as the waves from the sea they rise from. That may be an uncomfortable truth for some but, for me, the matter was settled.

"Until now. With the advent of song generation platforms, the thorny issue has been upended. At last, the artist can be separated from the art. Not just that, the artist — that flawed, messy, broken, woeful, joyful problem — can be removed from the equation altogether, like so much dross.

"(AI song generator) Suno, the Great Cancellator, which has never loved or laughed or grieved, never experienced joy or loss or heartbreak, never felt boredom or its adjacent epiphany, produces an imitation of the soul — a song — in fifteen seconds flat. This is an affront to any songwriter who has lived and struggled in this world and earned the right to create a song.

"Artificial Intelligence, Catherine, may save the world, annihilate it, or do something in between. I don't know. But song generator platforms are, in my view, indicators of this nascent technology's demonic potential to hollow out human endeavour and sever our connection to the divine.
"They mock creation itself by rendering humanity unnecessary, taking the fruits of human striving and reducing them to mere products. It is, perhaps, our final, most soul-destroying humiliation.

"For those eager to rid the world of problematic artists — for these censorious forces remain persistent — it is surely cause for celebration, as these platforms promise to rid the world of artists altogether.
"Love, Nick"
US and NZ elections point to the land of Oz
Great read, as always from Ian Verrender for your coffee break.
Brew it up, check it out.
This week: Business and consumer sentiment, US inflation
With thanks to our stalwart Monday blogger Stephen Letts, here's a look at what's to come this week.
Australia
Tue: NAB business survey (Oct), Westpac/MI consumer confidence (Oct), Life 360 Q3Wed: Loan approvals (Q3)Thu: MI Inflation expectations, Aristocrat FY, Orica FY
Tue: NAB business survey (Oct), Westpac/MI consumer confidence (Oct), Life 360 Q3
Wed: Loan approvals (Q3)
Thu: MI Inflation expectations, Aristocrat FY, Orica FY
International
Tue: CN – Trade balance (Oct)US – CPI (Oct), Small business optimism (Oct)Thu: UK – GDP (Q3)Fri: EU – GDP (Q3)
Tue: CN – Trade balance (Oct)
US – CPI (Oct), Small business optimism (Oct)
Thu: UK – GDP (Q3)
Fri: EU – GDP (Q3)
Locally, the interest this week will centre on readings of business and consumer sentiment out today.
NAB will publish its business survey of conditions and confidence for October, which is expected to show a further decline in sentiment amid rising interest rates.
Westpac’s reading of consumer confidence is also expected to be glummer for similar reasons.
The ABS publishes Q3 lending data on Wednesday, which is likely to show about a 9% decline in housing approvals, reflecting the impact of rate rises and tax changes.
In the US, the focus will be on October CPI inflation data (Tuesday), which is expected to show a 0.3% over the month rise in the headline CPI and core inflation at 0.2%.
Hot chip spy tale leads to court action
Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang have been sued in a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders.
The tale of the boss of the computer chip maker, and his entanglement with a suspected Chinese spy, has already led to its first court date.

A complaint filed in Federal Court in California alleges the defendants misled shareholders about Mr Huang's affair and did not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.
ASX 200 opens higher in first minutes of trading
As tipped by the futures market, the flagship ASX 200 index has opened higher.
The index, which tracks the value of the 200 largest companies listed on the Australian stock exchange, was up +0.7% or 63.4 points to 9,093 points.
Watch out for dodgy Black Friday deals
Bogus "countdown timers", false "storewide" discount claims and misleading price comparisons are all in the regulator's sights ahead of this year's Black Friday sales season.
As my colleague Jessica Irvine writes, it has prompted a warning from the consumer watchdog about a proliferation of illegal marketing tactics.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has expanded its annual "sweep" of Black Friday advertisements from retailer websites to also include social media posts and marketing emails.
"Consumers should be aware that a 'sale' sign doesn't always mean it's a good deal," warns ACCC deputy chair Catriona Lowe.
"We know some businesses use tactics to mislead consumers into thinking they are getting a bargain even when they are not."
Six Australian retailers, including Michael Hill and MyHouse, have been fined a collective $217,800 by the ACCC over the past two years for misleading advertising during the Black Friday sales.
Find more detail here
What happened overnight?
From Kyle Rodda of capital.com, here's a look at what went down (and up) overnight, ahead of our market opening shortly.
• Wall Street rebounds as investors buy into an inexpensive market
• Crude tumbles and boosts stock prices on easing geopolitical risk
• Market participants await a heavily compromised US CPI release

Wall Street roared back as market participants swept in to take advantage of a cheap market. The AI trade came back to life, ignoring the salacious Jensen Huang affair sideshow that weighed on Nvidia shares, after several weeks of selling pressure caused by weak quarterly earnings and regulatory risks stemming from US midterm elections.

Market sentiment was aided by another major drop in crude prices overnight. Crude extended its decline since the start of the month to nearly 20% as the geopolitical risk premium that drove prices higher in the first place is priced out. The move was aided by comments from US President Donald Trump over the weekend that he sees it as “unlikely” that there’ll be imminent strikes against Iran. The tumble in oil prices is broadly helping market sentiment and, along with expectations of a more moderate US fiscal impulse, easing the upside risk to global interest rates. The developments helped broaden out Wall Street’s overnight rally, spreading it beyond merely an AI recovery.

The critical risk event for the week lands tonight with US CPI data and could potentially upend Wall Street’s nascent recovery. The data itself is going to be very holey and may induce greater uncertainty depending on what the numbers reveal. The print will be without annual figures after the halt in data collection in October last year because of the US government shutdown. As a result, the month-over-month numbers are the only ones market participants will have at their disposal, with inferring annualised price growth all that can be done to get a sense of how year-over-year inflation could be tracking. Forecasters predict US headline CPI rose 0.3% last month and core lifted 0.2%, both of which are a moderation on last month’s numbers. This will be the last CPI release in the US before the Fed’s final meeting of 2026 next month. After Friday’s stronger-than-expected jobs data, the markets ascribe an 85% chance of a rate hike at that meeting.
Black Friday is approaching
Australians are forecast to spend a record $7.2 billion over the Black Friday-Cyber Monday weekend, according to new research from the Australian Retail Council (ARC) and Roy Morgan.
The data reveals a rise in shoppers chasing savings.
Spending across the four-day event from 27-30 November is tipped to rise 5.5% on last year, delivering an additional $374 million in sales.
• Black Friday shoppers plan to spend an average of $920 across the sales period, up $116 or 14.4% on 2025
• Almost one in three plans to spend $1,000 or more
ARC chief industry engagement officer Fleur Brown said pressure on household budgets was pushing the focus on value.

“Black Friday continues to rise in popularity in Australia and has become a major opportunity to buy Christmas gifts and planned purchases at discounted prices. With an unrelenting pressure on many household budgets, shoppers are looking to make their money go even further this year," she said.
The November/Christmas season is the busiest annual period for retailers.
DJs jobs in the balance

Australia's peak union body is pressing for the "maximum number of jobs to be saved" across David Jones department stores and for the protection of all workers’ financial and legal entitlements by the company’s administrators.
We're expecting to learn more this week.
Here's ACTU secretary, Melissa Donnelly:
“Workers across the country are standing in solidarity with DJs workers, while they face an anxious wait for updates on the company’s situation and the future of its stores."
The union boss says the administration of the retailer is the "first real test" of payday super laws.
"They are a lifeline, because DJs workers know that in the event of any redundancies, at least they can be secure in the knowledge that their super entitlements are paid up and protected.

“Before the payday super laws came in, workers risked losing up to three months of their super entitlements if their company faced financial insecurity, risked going into administration or from blatant employer super theft.

“This is not just a protection for DJs workers but for workers in any vulnerable company and one the union movement will be keeping a close watch on to ensure workers’ super and other entitlements are fully protected."
Market set to lift at 10am AEDT

Australian shares are poised to open higher on Tuesday, lifted by potential gains in the resources sub-index on stronger copper and gold prices, while broader strength might be hampered by losses in energy stocks following a slide in oil prices.
The local share price index futures rose 1.1%, a 100.3-point premium to the underlying S&P/ASX 200 index close.
The benchmark gained 0.1% on Monday.
Trading runs 10am to 4pm AEDT.
Geopolitical forecaster tips end of Iran war
Legendary geopolitical forecaster George Friedman joined The Business from the sidelines at the UBS Australasia conference in Sydney.
He says he can see the Ian war ending, but he also doesn't know how the conflict will resolve.
"It's almost certain very soon because both sides need to have it," he said, reflecting on the rising cost of the conflict on the US and Iran.
The "futurologist" observed that Australia is standing more on its own in the Pacific through allies like Japan and India, with whom it has developed a close military relationship.
"What we see evolving in this region is the same thing that's evolving in the Middle East. This isn't 1945, this isn't 1950 or 1960. Nations in this region have become much more mature and capable."
On AI, he thinks the extreme claims reflect overstatements by industry, but the fundamental reality of AI is here.
While he says the technology won't live up to the "preposterous" claims around it, what is needed now is investment.
"The process of maturing will cause problems," he observed.
Oil down more than $7 a barrel in post settlement trade as Trump signals restraint on Iran
• Trump says he is highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran
• Physical Brent trades below futures in sign of weaker market

Brent crude futures continued tumbling after settlement on Monday to lose more than $7 a barrel, hitting their lowest since late August, after US President Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran.
(All figures in this post are in US dollars)
Brent crude futures settled down $5.75, or 5.85%, at $92.57 a barrel. Prices continued falling after settlement and were last down more than $7 a barrel.
US West Texas Intermediate futures settled down $3.98, or 4.38%, to $86.85. US crude futures also continued falling, last down more than $5 in post-settlement trade.
The Brent benchmark plunged by 16% last week, its steepest weekly drop since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

On Sunday, Trump said he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed. Still, both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
"This seems to have encouraged sellers on the prospects for peace even while the actual fighting is not slowing down," TACenergy analysts said in a note.
Last week, Trump had hinted at a resumption of attacks on Iran and Tehran vowed to respond by striking US and Israeli targets. But there has been no sign of a large-scale US military operation.

A senior Iranian security official told the country's state media that Tehran has no plans to negotiate unless Washington takes practical steps to meet seven conditions set out in a June interim agreement.

Saudi Arabia's foreign minister and his Omani counterpart stressed in a phone call on Monday the need to press ahead with diplomatic efforts to contain the regional crisis and safeguard maritime security and sea lanes, Saudi state media reported.
On Monday, Trump will meet the prime minister of Qatar, which has been a mediator, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.

Iraq has reached understandings with the US to allow Iraqi oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near Oman, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera on Sunday.
"Crude futures are under selling pressure once again as oil volumes continue strong through the Strait of Hormuz," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice-president of trading at BOK Financial.

In the Medina region, a fire was extinguished after Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline was struck, an energy ministry source said, according to state media. There were no casualties and the pipeline's operations were not affected.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday it destroyed a factory used by the group to make ballistic missile components and a chemical plant used for producing ballistic missile fuel, without specifying the locations of the targets.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for an attack on Sunday at Saudi oil giant Aramco's corporate office in the heart of the financial district of the capital Riyadh. Debris from the attempted attack blew out windows across several floors, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.

"Fresh tanker incidents and an attack on Saudi Aramco’s offices show that shipping and regional security risks remain unresolved as traders price in a less disruptive outcome," said Gelber & Associates.
Elsewhere, Russia and Ukraine are coming to US-brokered talks to end Moscow's war on Ukraine with good intentions, a US official said on Monday.
In a briefing ahead of Tuesday's talks in Abu Dhabi, a US official told reporters that both sides had shown a little bit of flexibility privately on territorial issues.
Plenty of supply

Dated Brent, used to price cargoes around the world, has weakened to a discount to the nearby Brent futures contract, Morgan Stanley said in a report on Monday, highlighting weakness in the physical market.

The global oil market is showing signs of a return to excess supply as demand drops because of high prices, some analysts said. The global oil surplus is estimated at about 1.4 million barrels per day in October, JPMorgan said in a report last week.
OPEC oil output rose in October, a Reuters survey found, led by gains in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq despite continued constraints on exports.
Crude output from the 11-member Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries rose by 1.38 million bpd from the previous month to 22.87 million bpd, the survey found.
US crude oil and product stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Monday.
- Reuters
Before we start, let's catch up on yesterday
What happened yesterday? A lot.
Marcus Today senior analyst Henry Jennings says investors may need to get used to panic on global financial markets, following last week's market meltdown.
He says "volatility begets more volatility" and he does not think investors are "through the woods" yet. "I think this is something we have to get used to," Mr Jennings said.

"The markets have become far more gamified in some respects with computers, algorithmic trading, etc... you know once things get triggered and {tech} being a crowded trade as well, if everyone rushes to the exit at the same time and someone is shouting 'fire' it can get a little ugly to say the least."
Jennings warned "this is what panic looks like … and I think we're going to have to live with this a little while".
Meanwhile technology giant Nvidia says it's launching an independent investigation into claims its chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

Republicans have called on Mr Huang to brief the US Congress about allegations this month. Nvidia says its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but its inquiry would examine all available information.
More roadblocks for data centres
I found this fascinating in the wash-up of the US midterm elections.
The governor's office in each state is akin to our premiers or chief ministers. And no matter which party won, they were placing new restrictions on data centre builds.
New conditions include paying for grid upgrades, losing tax breaks, water limits and rules about labour (such as guaranteeing jobs).
Of almost 12,000 investors, who pumped more than $1 billion of their retirement savings into the First Guardian and Shield schemes, more than 6,000 were clients of advisers under InterPrac.
An astonishing series of reports from Nassim Khadem is worth your time.

These 6,000 clients put about $680 million into the two funds on the advice of financial planners licensed under InterPrac. They are now worried that the sale of InterPrac to Bellbird Australia could shrink the pool of money available to compensate them.
The corporate regulator is considering whether there are grounds to stop the sale.
ASIC is also suing InterPrac, which is the only solvent financial advice licensee with exposure to the collapsed investment funds.

Meanwhile, Meredith Wright is fighting to recover almost $200,000 of her husband Kevin's superannuation, as he battles lung cancer. She has gone to the financial ombudsman AFCA, to make a compensation claim against the firm that oversaw the adviser who gave them the advice.
"I just want Kevin's money back, it's his money."
Loading...
Richard Orr lost money after being contacted by a telemarketer, who put him in touch with a financial adviser, also licensed by InterPrac.
The 54-year-old has pancreatic cancer and wants to provide for his family when he's not around. More than $200,000 of his retirement savings was moved into First Guardian.
"I don't care about anything else, but for me I've got to fight …" he said.

At the same time the corporate cop ASIC is warning licensees about their use of unlicensed telemarketers that lure Australians into switching savings, and in some cases, discuss investment performance.

Under the law, only a licensed financial planner can give advice about investments. The federal government recently banned telemarketers who cold call. Now, there are pleas to ensure it's properly policed.

"I think we need to monitor how that ban occurs, and success or otherwise, and consider the activities of those who do have licences because we've seen some egregious breaches in this area and people have suffered" Liberal senator Paul Scarr says.
Shares of Nvidia tumble more than 5 per cent on spy scandal
It's the biggest business story in the world and it won't be going away today.
The computer chip maker opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort".

Nvidia's announcement of the investigation followed Mr Huang's acknowledgement that he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, US intelligence determined was gathering information for China.
China's Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations as a smear campaign against Beijing.
NEXTDC pauses uncontracted projects after Australian data centre woes
NEXTDC boss Craig Scroggie is in a world of pain.
A community dispute has disrupted a big build, causing the share price to crater. That low price enticed a rival to buy almost 10% of the stock.
He told a conference late yesterday winning community support had become the company's top priority.
NEXTDC had previously said it would stop work on all projects without customer contracts following a big setback on a facility in the inner-west of Melbourne.

"The last couple of weeks [I] certainly didn't expect to be in the position we're in today having to deal with some delays," NEXTDC's chief executive, Craig Scroggie, told the UBS Australasia conference.

"That's unfortunately probably reflective of the global environment in relation to the engagement, social licence, people's feelings about artificial intelligence and data centres being the physical embodiment of that."

Scroggie said the M3 delay meant the top priority was to win community backing for that project and "anything that didn't have a customer contract and a customer commitment that we absolutely have to deliver on is now no longer a priority".
The company previously announced it would pause projects where it didn't have a customer signed up to take on the "compute" created by it.
He did not say how many projects would be paused. The company had 11 centres in development or in the planning stages, according to its 2026 annual report.
"That work can't restart until we clearly communicate that we've solved this problem, that we've earned the trust of everybody that's been supporting us, and then we will get back to work."
NEXTDC's rivals Goodman Group and its New York-listed partner, Digital Realty bought a 9.9% stake in the company last week following the share price plunge.
"When you have a challenge like we've had in the last couple of weeks, it's not really any surprise to me that people … look at that and say, now might be the time," Scroggie said.

Goodman and Digital Realty said they had no plans at the moment to launch a takeover offer, but reserved the right to do so. They said they would "look forward to a potential collaboration with the NEXTDC board and management on the ways and forms in which the parties may help to address the challenges facing the company".
Following their share raid, NEXTDC's share price recovered the ground lost from the earnings writedown.
The company has its annual general meeting in 10 days.
- with Reuters
Wall St jumps back as oil slide eases inflation worries
Big night on US markets. Here's a quick summary:
• S&P on track for biggest daily gain in seven months
• Nvidia down as company probes foreign intelligence effort claims
• KKR up after record quarterly profit

US stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 bounce off its biggest weekly drop since April 2025, and tech shares jumped even as AI heavyweight Nvidia slumped with controversy swirling around CEO Jensen Huang.
Last week, stocks slumped after a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.
Each of the 11 major S&P 500 sector indexes rose on Monday. Industrials and consumer discretionary were the top performers, rising more than 3%.
Nvidia falls despite broader gains

Markets were in rally mode even as Nvidia, the second-most-valuable company in the world, tumbled about 6% and hit its lowest intraday level since March 31, on questions about CEO Huang's future at the AI chipmaker, after an internal investigation into whether a foreign intelligence effort had targeted him.
Here's the take of Ken Polcari, partner and chief market strategist at SlateStone Wealth in Jupiter, Florida:

"The AI story is not going away if people are worried about that, the Democrats are not going to destroy AI. They can't. It's got a life of its own. They can put regulation around it, but they're certainly not stopping it."
Providing further support was a sharp drop in crude oil prices that helped dampen concerns about price pressures, as US President Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran.
"Oil prices for sure, if they're down 4%, that's certainly adding fuel to the fire," Polcari said.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,131.81 points, or 2.21%, to 52,417.54, the S&P 500 gained 177.81 points, or 2.41%, to 7,554.67 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 656.06 points, or 2.67%, to 25,235.49.
The S&P was on track for its biggest daily percentage gain since April 8, while the Nasdaq was on pace for its best day since July 30.
Inflation readings are on the docket this week as the Labor Department will release its Consumer Price Index report for October on Tuesday and Producer Price Index on Friday.
Analysts see over-reaction

Some analysts on Wall Street also viewed last week's decline as an overreaction. Morgan Stanley and UBS said last week's rout in AI stocks was overdone, and the risks of extreme regulation of data centre developments under a Democratic-controlled Congress were unlikely to play out.
But there are other challenges. Fears of a December rate hike persisted following October's stronger-than-expected jobs data.

Chipmakers surged. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose more than 6% after plunging more than 12% last week, its biggest weekly drop since the week ended April 4, 2025. Nvidia was the sole decliner in the index, while Broadcom was up nearly 9%, and Advanced Micro Devices surged about 13% as the two biggest boosts.

Shares of investment giant KKR advanced 1.9% after its quarterly profit hit a record high. Constellation Energy, an energy firm with exposure to the AI buildout, shot up more than 10% after its adjusted third-quarter profit surpassed expectations.
Berkshire Hathaway's class A shares gained 0.6% after the conglomerate reported lower third-quarter profit.
- Reuters

What's going on?

Nvidia spy scandal: hot chips and illicit affairs
Bombshell story from yesterday, still dominating world news.
Nvidia, the company at the centre of the global AI build-out, has launched an independent investigation after reports its CEO Jensen Huang was allegedly targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation.
That's one way of putting it, with the CEO admitting he had an affair outside of his marriage.
What could the allegations, and the investigation now underway, mean for one of the world’s most valuable companies?
Carrington Clarke and ABC Business reporter Stephanie Chalmers break it all down on the most recent episode of Business Daily.
